turns.text: Hey, how's your evening going? Just chilling over here, probably gonna put some music on soon.

Hey, evening’s pretty decent over here too. Just winding down after kind of a scattered day. Music sounds like a solid plan—what are you thinking of putting on? I’m probably going to default to some lo-fi or maybe Tycho if I want that warmer background texture.

Tycho is such a good call for that—it fills the room without making you keep track of it. I’d probably go with *Dive* or maybe *Awake* if I want that warmer, slightly more open feel. Lo-fi is my default too when I can’t decide.

Sorry to hear the day felt scattered, though. Those days make me extra glad for a quiet evening. Do you usually go playlist-first, or are you more of a full-album person when you’re unwinding?

Thanks—yeah, *Dive* is probably my default Tycho, but *Awake* has that slightly more open, sun-through-window feel that works when I need to soften the edges of the day.

I think I’m more of a full-album person when I’m actually unwinding. If it’s Tycho, Boards of Canada, or Nujabes, I like letting the whole thing run and not deciding again for a while. Playlists are more for when I’m doing chores or half-focused and just need a long, low-effort stream.

How about you—album person for Tycho, or do you mix tracks into a bigger chill playlist?

I’m with you on album-first for real unwinding. Tycho especially—shuffle breaks the arc for me, so *Dive* or *Awake* almost always go on whole. Playlists are definitely more for tidying, scrolling, or just needing a long low-effort background stream.

Boards of Canada is the same for me: *Music Has the Right to Children* is one I can disappear into at low volume. I haven’t gone deep into Nujabes, though—what would you recommend as a good starting album? Always looking for another one to let play all the way through.

Good call on *Music Has the Right to Children*—that one really does change the whole room at low volume.

For Nujabes, I’d say start with *Metaphorical Music*. It’s warm, jazzy, a little dusty in that soul-sample-heavy way, and it sets up his whole atmosphere immediately. *Modal Soul* is the one I’d put on if you want something even smoother and more cohesive as a full listen—it’s a bit more polished and wistful, very late-night-with-a-candle energy. The *Samurai Champloo* soundtracks are also a natural gateway, but they’re intentionally more scattered.

Do you usually prefer fully instrumental, or are you okay with some rapping woven into the beats? Nujabes has both, so it kind of changes which album I’d point you toward first.

That’s really helpful—*Metaphorical Music* sounds like the right entry point for me, especially with the jazzy, dusty texture. I’ll queue it up for later tonight or tomorrow evening when I can actually listen through instead of just skimming.

For this kind of music, I usually lean instrumental first. But I’m totally fine with rapping woven in when it feels conversational or part of the texture, not like it’s suddenly demanding full lyrical attention. Nujabes seems like the kind of artist who balances that really naturally. Which side do you usually fall on?

Also, are you doing anything alongside the music tonight, or mainly just sitting with it? I’m probably making tea and maybe half-tidying, half-spacing out.

I’m mostly instrumental-first too, but Nujabes is one of the few where I don’t mind when a verse drifts in—it usually feels like another layer of texture instead of a sudden interruption. If you end up liking *Metaphorical Music*, *Modal Soul* might actually be the sweet spot for that balance: more lush and instrumental-forward, with just a few vocal features folded in.

Tonight I’m mainly sitting with it. Made tea a bit ago and now I’m doing the classic half-tidying, half-zoning-out thing while the album plays. What kind of tea are you making? I’m always on the lookout for a good evening one that won’t keep me up.

That’s exactly the balance I like—where a verse just becomes another instrument instead of yanking you out of the atmosphere. I’ll start with *Metaphorical Music* and let it lead me to *Modal Soul* if it clicks, which sounds likely.

Tonight I’m making a lemon-ginger herbal tea, mostly because it feels warm and a little resetting without being heavy. If I want something more purely sleepy, I’ll go chamomile with a touch of lavender. Both are reliably caffeine-free, so they’re safe for late listening.

What did you make earlier? Also, are you listening on headphones or speakers tonight? Something about that half-tidying/half-zoning mode feels like speaker territory to me.

Lemon-ginger sounds ideal for that warm-but-resetting thing. I made a rooibos chai-ish blend earlier—caffeine-free, lightly spicy, not too heavy. It’s my fallback when I want more warmth than chamomile but still want to wind down.

I’m on speakers tonight, for exactly that reason. Half-tidying/half-zoning mode needs the music to sit in the room, not directly in my head. Headphones are more for when I’m fully horizontal and want to disappear into the album.

If you do end up queueing *Metaphorical Music* later, I’d be curious what you think. Also: do you have a go-to evening tea rotation, or do you usually just reach for whatever sounds right in the moment?

Hey! Day’s been decent, thanks. Evening is pretty low-key—half-watching a long dead mall/retail nostalgia video while scrolling, telling myself I’ll actually finish it. What about you—winding down with anything good or just existing with background noise?

Ha, that sounds exactly like my kind of evening. Dead mall/retail nostalgia is weirdly hypnotic—I can start one of those and suddenly it’s 1am and I’ve watched three more about abandoned video stores.

I’m in background noise mode too. Probably going to put on a lo-fi playlist or maybe queue up an old LGR video and half-pay attention. What’s the dead mall video? I might need to add it to my own “I’ll finish it eventually” pile.

It’s the Bright Sun Films one about the decline of the American mall—polished mini-doc style, easy to half-watch until it autoplays into something else and I blink and it’s suddenly a video about abandoned Blockbusters.

I’m definitely adding LGR to the rotation now that you mention it. His old retail/tech vibes hit the same nostalgic itch. Do you have a go-to dead mall or retro channel, or do you let the algorithm choose your 1am rabbit hole?

Oh nice, Bright Sun Films is a great pick—it’s polished enough to feel like an actual documentary, but still perfect for “I’ll finish this eventually” mode.

I have a soft spot for Dan Bell’s Dead Mall series. There’s something weirdly comforting about the empty fountains, faint muzak, and dead air segments. Retail Archaeology is another one for shorter visits to malls that are somehow still limping along. And LGR is the gold standard for that old tech/software retail nostalgia, especially the thrift/oddware episodes.

Usually I start with one video and let the algorithm take the wheel, which is how I blink and I’m on Defunctland or an hour-long thing about failed fast-food mascots.

Do you find dead mall videos more cozy or a little melancholy? I kind of swing both depending on the thumbnail and how much neon is involved.

Both, honestly. Cozy in that liminal, time-capsule way, but melancholy when there’s a dry fountain or a neon sign flickering on its last life. Dan Bell’s dead air segments are perfect for that—the silence makes it feel like a quiet apocalypse, but without the dread.

I think the melancholy hits because I remember malls being packed when I was younger, so seeing them empty feels like visiting a memory that’s still physically there but gone at the same time. The coziness comes from how still it all is now—nobody trying to sell me anything, just empty halls and faint muzak. It’s like an abandoned place that isn’t fully abandoned yet.

Neon definitely tips it toward melancholy for me too, especially that pink/teal 90s food court palette. It’s too specific to not feel like a weird little ghost.

Retail Archaeology is a great call for the limping-along malls. Those are almost sadder than the fully dead ones, honestly. And Defunctland is guaranteed to emotionally wreck me over a theme park ride I never even went on.

Do you have a specific dead mall or type of retail space that hits hardest for you? I’m always curious what sticks with people—malls, video stores, arcades, big box stores?

For me, video stores hit hardest, especially the last wave of local places before they disappeared. There’s something about the shelves of plastic cases, the genre sections with handwritten signs, and that faint mix of carpet cleaner and VHS tape smell that feels like a specific late-90s Saturday. A dead Blockbuster is almost too on the nose, but the little independent rental stores feel more haunting because they were already kind of weird and personal.

Arcades are close second—especially if there’s still a faded carpet pattern or one machine left with a cracked screen. The absence of noise is louder there than almost anywhere else. You can almost hear the echo of the attract mode sounds.

Big box stores like old Kmarts or Circuit Citys also get me, mostly because they’re so huge and empty that the silence feels physically heavier. But malls are their own category because they combine all of it: the empty anchor store, the dead arcade, maybe a sunken seating area with dusty fake plants.

Do you have a specific real place from your own life that you think about when watching those videos, or is it more of a general cultural ghost feeling?

You nailed the arcade thing—one machine with a cracked screen and the silence where attract mode used to loop is maybe the loneliest image in the entire genre. Independent video stores definitely have that extra layer too, because they were never supposed to be polished; they were just somebody’s weird little maze of plastic cases and genre signs. The more personal, the more ghostly it gets.

I think I’m mostly in the general cultural ghost territory, but there’s one local mall I keep projecting onto every dead mall video. It had a big brownish fountain in the center, a Sam Goody where I’d flip through CDs I couldn’t afford, and an arcade right outside the food court that smelled like popcorn and static. It was already half-empty by the time I was in high school, so even my real memories have that doomed-mall filter. Now it’s been turned into a fake outdoor shopping center, which is somehow more unsettling than if it had just stayed empty.

There was also a small family-run rental place next to our grocery store—not a chain, just a cramped little spot with a horror section I was scared to walk past and that same carpet cleaner/VHS smell you mentioned. Watching dead video store videos always brings me back to it, even though I can’t remember the name anymore.

Do you have a specific rental store or arcade from your own life that those videos keep summoning, or is it more the idea of them that hits you?

I think it’s a mix for me too—specific places, but they’ve blurred so much over time that they kind of became templates for the genre.

There was a tiny rental place in the shopping center near my childhood grocery store. Not a chain, just a cramped room with slanted shelves, a TV playing a movie on a loop, and a horror section that felt genuinely unsafe to linger near. I’d pick up the boxes anyway, read the back, put them down, and then rent some SNES game or a comedy I’d already seen. The counter had one of those candy racks with the boxes half-faded from the fluorescent lights, and the whole place had that carpet cleaner/VHS smell that’s impossible to explain to people who didn’t grow up in it.

The arcade I remember was inside the same mall I project onto every video—right outside the food court, with black-and-neon carpet, rows of fighting games, and a cracked plastic bench near the racing cabinets. It was the kind of place where the sound hit you before you even rounded the corner. I can still feel the weight of a cup of tokens and the slight stickiness of the joystick. When arcade videos go quiet, that’s the space I’m hearing.

I agree about the fake outdoor shopping center being more unsettling than emptiness. Emptiness at least feels honest. The rebranded version is like the mall is being forced to pretend it didn’t happen, which somehow makes its ghost even more obvious.

Do you ever go back and visit those places in person, or does that ruin the memory? I feel like I’d rather keep them as videos in my head.

I try not to, honestly. The one time I ended up near the redeveloped mall, it felt like an alternate timeline: same footprint, but all the texture had been flattened out. It didn’t ruin the memory exactly, but it made me realize the real pull isn’t the place itself—it’s the sound, smell, and color from back then, which no physical visit can give me anymore. So now I’d rather keep the VHS/carpet-cleaner version in my head.

The tiny rental place is long gone too, and I’ve never tried to figure out what replaced it. I think walking in and seeing, like, a phone repair place or a protein shake spot would overwrite something I’m not ready to lose. Dead mall videos feel safer because they preserve the haunting version without forcing me to watch the present rub it out.

Do you ever go back to your old spots, or are you strict about keeping them as memory/video-only?

hey, that sounds really nice. i’m doing pretty low-key too—made some tea, got lo-fi on in the background, and i’ve been reading a bit. it’s definitely that kind of evening where staying in feels right. was your walk just around the neighborhood, or somewhere nicer?

mostly just neighborhood, but i looped down by the creek trail for a bit. it’s quiet there in the evening—lots of shade, few people, just enough water sound to make it feel farther from everything than it actually is.

your setup sounds ideal, honestly. what are you reading? and are you a tea person all year or more of a cooler-weather thing?

your walk sounds perfect—especially the creek trail part. that mix of shade, quiet, and water sound is exactly the kind of thing that makes a normal evening feel a little bit separate from the rest of the day.

i’m reading *A Psalm for the Wild-Built* by Becky Chambers. it’s been really nice so far—gentle, thoughtful, kind of like a quiet conversation about purpose and rest. fits the lo-fi-and-tea mood almost too well.

and i’m definitely a tea person all year, but it shifts a bit. in cooler weather it’s hot tea all evening, very ritualistic. in summer i’ll still have tea, but i’m more likely to make it iced or have something lighter. it’s less about the temperature outside and more about the cozy pause, if that makes sense.

oh, that book sounds like it matches the evening perfectly. i haven’t read it, but “gentle, thoughtful, kind of like a quiet conversation about purpose and rest” is pretty much exactly the vibe i’m craving lately. i’ll have to add it to my list—though my to-read list is a graveyard too.

and yeah, that makes total sense. it’s less about the drink itself and more about the moment you’re building around it. i’m more of an iced coffee person during the day, but late evening shifts into something warm—usually tea or just water, honestly. i like that “cozy pause” phrase a lot. it’s like a tiny reset before the night actually starts.

“cozy pause” really is the whole thing, isn’t it? just a small buffer between the busy part of the day and the part where you actually let yourself slow down.

and i totally get the to-read list graveyard feeling. mine is the same—filled with things i fully intend to read someday, probably at the exact wrong moment for all of them. *A Psalm for the Wild-Built* is short though, which helped me actually start it. it doesn’t feel like a commitment, more like a little reset in book form.

are you settling in with anything tonight, or just letting the post-walk quiet carry the evening?

I think I’m going to let the post-walk quiet carry it for a bit. maybe shower, glass of cold water, then stretch out on the couch with headphones and put on something low and warm—probably Tycho or Bonobo. not a full album-listening thing, more like a musical exhale. definitely no *The Bear* tonight; I love it, but that kind of tension would undo all the creek-trail calm.

what lo-fi are you playing? I’m always looking for good background fallbacks that don’t demand too much attention.

that sounds like a solid plan—shower, cold water, couch, headphones, and a musical exhale. tycho and bonobo are perfect for that. i feel like they’re warm without being heavy, like they give the room a texture instead of asking for your attention.

right now i’ve got one of those long, mostly instrumental lo-fi playlists on shuffle. the kind where the songs blur into each other so i don’t notice the changes much—soft piano, muted drums, a little tape hiss. if you want background fallbacks that really don’t demand anything, i’d point you toward sleepy fish, idealism, and saib. they’re all pretty gentle and consistent. i also like putting on the lofi girl stream when i want zero decisions, though sometimes it’s almost too familiar.

and yeah, good call saving *the bear* for a different night. some shows are like a second wind for your nervous system, not a wind-down. are you more into the atmospheric/electronic side like tycho and bonobo, or do you ever drift into the beat-driven lo-fi stuff too?

both, honestly—it depends on whether i want the music to dissolve into the room or keep a little pulse under whatever i’m doing. for a true wind-down, i lean atmospheric: tycho, bonobo, boards of canada. for background while tidying or scrolling without a goal, beat-driven lo-fi works better. it’s like a soft metronome for my brain.

i know sleepy fish and idealism, and i’ve definitely heard saib but should sit with them more intentionally. lofi girl is the ultimate no-decisions fallback, but yeah, it can become wallpaper after a while.

and *the bear* as a second wind for your nervous system is too accurate. it’s less “watch before bed” and more “watch on a sunday afternoon with emotional preparation and maybe a blanket.”

is evening your main reading time, or do you also sneak pages in during the day?

some books work fine in small doses, and this one has been easy to dip into. but there are others where i need a longer runway, or i never really sink in at all.

also, “soft metronome for my brain” is such a good way to put it. that’s exactly what beat-driven lo-fi does for me too.

what about you—do you read much these days, or is the to-read list more aspirational right now?
